m.c: May the hope of the resurrection fill your heart with peace and courage throughout this day. Walk without fear, for the Lord of life goes before you. May his blessing accompany you every hour. May God keep you always.
h: On this day, November 22, 1963, the Christian writer Clive Staples Lewis, known around the world as C. S. Lewis, died at his home in Oxford, England. He was one week short of his sixty-fifth birthday. His house was called The Kilns, and he had spent much of his adult life there.

That same day, the whole world had its eyes on other news: the assassination of United States President John F. Kennedy. That is why Lewis’s death went almost unnoticed in the headlines. Yet his books continued to speak for decades. For years he had been a convinced atheist, and he came to the Christian faith already as an adult. He then defended it with clarity and simplicity in works such as “Mere Christianity” and “The Screwtape Letters,” and told it imaginatively in “The Chronicles of Narnia,” where the lion Aslan reflects the goodness and power of Christ.

Lewis also knew sorrow. He lost his mother as a child, and in 1960 his wife, Joy Davidman, died. He wrote honestly about that grief. Yet he never ceased to point to the Christian hope: that this life is not the end and that God is preparing something better for those who love him.

His passing reminds us of what Jesus taught the Sadducees: God is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to him all are alive. For those who are in Christ, the last day of earthly life is a door, not a wall. This hope is what Lewis sought to communicate all his life, with simple words and examples that anyone could understand, whatever their age or education.
m: Talking about death is not pleasant, but the Bible does not hide it. The life of C. S. Lewis, his grief, and his hope invite us to look calmly at what God promises us. Isaiah announced that the Lord will swallow up death forever and wipe away the tears from all faces. It is a promise for those who hope in him.

First, live in gratitude. Every morning is a gift, not a guarantee. Before you begin your tasks, give thanks for your family, your health, and your work. Do not wait until it is too late to tell someone you love them.

Second, rest in the promise. When Jesus spoke with the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection, he reminded them that Moses calls the Lord “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” and that God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. If you are carrying a loss today, do not carry it alone. Weeping is not a lack of faith; Jesus himself wept at the tomb of his friend.

Third, use your time well. Lewis wrote steadily, day after day, and his words continue to serve thousands of people. Perhaps you will not write books, but you can leave good footprints: a kind word, a prayer for someone, a task well done. What is done out of love for God is never lost. Go out today with the certainty that the Lord is our salvation, and that we will rejoice and be glad in him. May this hope be your strength.
o: Eternal Father, we praise you at the beginning of this day, for you are the God of the living and not of the dead. You gave us life and you hold our days in your hands. Thank you, because in Christ death does not have the last word, and because you have given us a living hope that lights up even the darkest moments.

Today we ask you to teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom. Free us from worry over passing things and from anxiety over what we cannot control. Help us to love those near us while we have time, to say what needs to be said, and to forgive what needs to be forgiven. May we not put off gratitude or reconciliation until tomorrow.

Comfort those who mourn a loved one today. Be their refuge and remind them that you will wipe away the tears from all faces. Give us faith to believe your promises, even when we do not yet see their fulfillment. May our works, our words, and our labor today bear witness that we hope in you. Guide us by your Spirit and be our strength yourself. May your peace guard our hearts today. In Jesus’ name, amen.
m.s: The Passing of C. S. Lewis

t.c: Thank you, Father, for one more day under your care. Hand over tonight your burdens and your faults, for his grace covers them. Rest quietly in the embrace of the one who never ceases to love you. May your sleep be sweet and your heart at peace.
h: Jesus told a parable about a father who had two sons. The younger asked for his share of the inheritance, went off to a far country, and squandered all his money there, living unwisely. When a great famine arose, he began to be in need. He ended up feeding pigs and longing to be filled with the food they ate.

Then, Jesus said, he came to himself. He remembered that in his father’s house even the hired servants had bread in abundance. He decided to go back and prepared a few words: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son; treat me as one of your hired servants.”

But the father saw him while he was still far off. He was moved with compassion, ran, threw his arms around his neck, and kissed him. The son began his speech, but the father did not even let him finish. He ordered his servants to bring the best robe, a ring for his hand, and sandals for his feet. He had the fattened calf killed for a feast, for, he said, “this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.”

Jesus told this story to show us what God is like. He is not a judge waiting with arms crossed, but a Father who watches the road and runs to meet us. The door is never closed to the one who decides to return. The prophet Isaiah had announced it: let the wicked forsake his way and return to the LORD, who will have mercy on him, for he will abundantly pardon. It was the greatest of all Jesus’ parables about mercy, and those who heard it for the first time understood that the heart of God rejoices more over a homecoming than over anything else in the world.
m: This parable speaks to us whether we have been the son who left or the one who stayed at home. At nightfall, it is a good time to ask ourselves: is there something today that distances me from my Father’s heart? God does not seek our perfection, he seeks our return.

First, come to yourself, as the young man did. Spend a few minutes in silence and review your day honestly. If there was a word or action that did not please God, acknowledge it. No long speech is needed. The son had prepared one, but the father welcomed him before he finished it. Forgiveness awaits us even before we have finished asking for it.

Second, accept the embrace. Many believers return to God but go on feeling like hired servants. The father restored his son’s place: robe, ring, and sandals. If God has forgiven you, stop punishing yourself. Receiving his grace is also a way of honoring him.

Third, imitate the father. Perhaps someone in your family or church needs a gesture of forgiveness from you today. Write a message, make a call, or at the very least pray for that person. And before you sleep, give thanks, because there is joy in heaven over every sinner who repents. Sleep in peace: you are loved as a son or daughter. May this assurance go with you as you close your eyes. God never tires of welcoming you, and his door is open at every hour of the night.
o: Good Father, at the end of this day, we come to give you thanks. You have waited for us with patience, like the father who watches the road every evening. Thank you, because you do not treat us according to our sins and, when we return to you, you run to welcome us. Your love is greater than our faults and your forgiveness wider than our shame.

We acknowledge that today, at one moment or another, we strayed from your will. Perhaps through a harsh word, a proud thought, or an omission that could have helped someone. We ask your forgiveness. Thank you, because you abundantly pardon and because in Christ there is no condemnation for those who trust in him. Cleanse us and renew in us a grateful heart.

Tonight we entrust to you all those who have wandered from you and from their homes. Bring back the children who are far away, heal broken relationships, and teach us to welcome with joy the one who returns. Take rancor from us and make us merciful as you are merciful. We rest on your grace and sleep in your peace, knowing that tomorrow your compassions will be new. Thank you for loving us as we are. In Jesus’ name, amen.
